item.title: GT Voice: Japan can't diversify its way out of losing Chinese tourists
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 00:15:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT With Chinese arrivals falling sharply, Japan's tourism industry is having to look for new sources of visitors. Nikkei Asia reported on Sunday that Japan was stepping up efforts to attract Indian visitors, with hotels and travel agencies expanding services tailored to them, including meal options and activities. India is indeed an expanding source of visitors for Japan. According to the Japan National Tourism Organization, arrivals from India rose 19 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026. Some other markets also posted strong growth. Yet Japan's broader tourism figures tell a less encouraging story: total international arrivals fell 2.9 percent over the same period. The decline in Chinese arrivals shows the limits of diversification. In the first nine months of 2026, the number of visitors from the Chinese mainland fell 55.5 percent year-on-year, a drop of more than 4 million. That is a substantial loss for a country that received just 30.7 million international visitors over the same period. It seems that Japan's sustained efforts to diversify its visitor base have so far failed to fill the gap left by Chinese tourists. Diversifying its visitor base makes sense for Japan, but that does not mean it can afford to let Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's erroneous remarks on Taiwan alienate Chinese tourists, given China's longstanding importance as a source market. Japan's Jiji Press reported in March that as Chinese arrivals declined amid strained relations, the Japanese government planned to focus on attracting more visitors from Europe, the US, Australia and other regions. If the strategy is judged by whether it can significantly boost Japan's overall inbound visitor numbers, it has failed so far. Japan's inbound visitor numbers will need to grow substantially, from about 42.7 million in 2025 to 60 million by 2030, to meet the government's target. Reaching that goal will be considerably more difficult if Chinese tourists remain a missing piece of Japan's tourism growth picture. Japan's inbound visitor numbers grew by 15.8 percent in 2025, with Asia accounting for part of that growth. As Asian economies continue to expand, more people in the region have the means and the appetite to travel abroad, creating new opportunities for destinations such as Japan. This trend was reflected in the first nine months of 2026, when arrivals from South Korea, India, Malaysia and Indonesia all rose by double digits. Yet this growing demand failed to translate into an increase in Japan's overall visitor numbers. Japan was well-placed to benefit from Asia's expanding appetite for overseas travel, but the steep decline in Chinese arrivals has left much of that potential unrealized. Chinese mainland residents made 148.36 million outbound tourist trips in 2025, up 20.8 percent year-on-year. Chinese outbound tourism is becoming an increasingly important source of visitors for destinations throughout Asia. Japan, with its own ambitions for tourism growth, can ill afford to turn its back on a market of this scale. Restoring Chinese tourists' confidence in visiting Japan will take more than promotional campaigns. Japan must address the damage caused by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's erroneous remarks on Taiwan, which lie at the root of the current situation in China-Japan relations. Consider this: when choosing where to spend their holidays, how many Chinese tourists would willingly travel to a destination where they feel their national sentiments have been deeply hurt? The answer is unlikely to be many. Those in Japan who expect visitor diversification to drive overall tourism growth and help the country reach its target of 60 million international arrivals by 2030 may be disappointed if they believe the Chinese market can simply be replaced. Diversification can broaden Japan's visitor base, but it cannot make the loss of such a large market any less consequential. Rebuilding Chinese tourists' confidence and regaining their goodwill are not optional extras. They are steps Japan's tourism industry can hardly afford to avoid if the country is serious about making meaningful progress toward its 2030 tourism target.

item.title: Worried about being 'snubbed' at APEC meeting? Tokyo has a guilty conscience: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 00:01:00
Illustration: Liu Rui/GT If today's Japan were genuinely contributing to regional prosperity and had earned the recognition of its neighbors, would it really need to be so suspicious? Tokyo's unease, in fact, shows Japan knows full well what role it is playing today. Japanese media have recently cited unnamed sources as saying that the Japanese government is seeking assurances from China that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will not be "snubbed" by the Chinese side at the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting. According to these reports, Tokyo is concerned that any "unusual plan" or public criticism of Japan by China could be seen as an attempt to "embarrass" Takaichi, in which case Japan would lodge a protest. It is obvious that these "unnamed sources " were not speaking mainly to the Chinese side when they chose to make such remarks to the media. By sending out signals through the press ahead of the APEC meeting that it is seeking assurances, Tokyo appears to have at least two objectives. First, it wants to give itself a convenient excuse in advance and satisfy hardline voters at home: If Japan is snubbed on the international stage, the blame should lie with China, not with the consequences of the Takaichi administration's own policies. Second, it attempts to shape the narrative for the international community in advance, indirectly framing any deterioration in relations as a sign of China's alleged failure to act with the magnanimity expected of a major power. This is a familiar tactic from Japan. At the same time, the extensive attention Japanese media have devoted in recent days to the question of how Takaichi might be treated at the upcoming meeting is telling in its own right. Why has an event that should be focused on cooperation across the Asia-Pacific come to be viewed by some in Japan as a minefield of potential snubs and slights? The answer likely lies in Japan's own words and actions over the past period. Since taking office, Takaichi has repeatedly sought to blur Japan's responsibility for its history of aggression, accelerated efforts to push beyond the principle of its "exclusively defense-oriented policy," and repeatedly crossed lines on the Taiwan question by invoking the notion of a "Taiwan contingency." These moves have seriously undermined the political foundations of China-Japan relations. In truth, Tokyo's current anxiety stems from its fear that its own actions may eventually carry consequences in a multilateral diplomatic setting. This is a textbook case of a government with a guilty conscience. Japan is pushing constitutional revision, expanding its military capabilities and whitewashing its history of aggression at home, while worrying that it might be "snubbed" at multilateral events abroad. This concern itself points to a fundamental mismatch between its policies and its expectations. In reality, a country's standing in regional affairs ultimately depends on what it can contribute to common development and whether it can convince its neighbors that its commitments are credible. Japan has long been an important participant in Asia-Pacific trade and investment, and a beneficiary of the postwar international order. If today's Japan were genuinely contributing to regional prosperity and had earned the recognition of its neighbors, would it really need to be so suspicious? Tokyo's unease, in fact, shows Japan knows full well what role it is playing today. In fact, for Japan, what truly earns it respect on the international stage is not any "guarantee" demanded in advance, but its own concrete actions. APEC focuses on development and cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region. Its core agenda has always centered on trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, supply chain resilience, the digital economy, green transformation and other issues. Reducing the core concerns of APEC participants to questions such as "Will I be treated differently?" or "Will I end up on the menu?" fundamentally narrows and distorts the nature of APEC. It also reflects Japan's distorted view of international relations today. Such thinking not only underestimates the composure and resolve of other members but also exposes Japan's anxiety about its own position. In the long term, this distorted worldview and set of values will further weaken Japan's position in regional cooperation. Asia-Pacific economic integration is entering a new phase driven by the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the vision of a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, with participating economies placing greater emphasis on regulatory consistency and policy continuity. When a country's leader devotes substantial political energy to breaking through established constraints and stirring up sensitive issues, other members will naturally reassess the political risks of deepening cooperation with that country. APEC is not a mechanism for punishment, but neither is it obligated to cover up any country's embarrassing conduct. If Japan continues to turn its domestic political needs into external provocations and then blames others for the resulting diplomatic setbacks, it will only further erode its credibility in regional affairs. What Japan should truly be concerned about is not the opportunity for a handshake or the seating arrangement for a group photo at a particular meeting, but how its misguided policies are steadily eroding the trust of neighboring countries, ultimately leaving it with increasingly limited diplomatic options. On China-Japan relations, China's position has remained consistent: The two sides must return to the spirit of the agreements reached in 1972. Rather than trapping itself within constraints of its own making, Japan should seriously reflect on its understanding of history, policies toward China and regional strategy, stop taking actions that undermine regional peace and stability or harm other countries' core interests, and demonstrate genuine sincerity in pursuing cooperation. It should stop pretending not to understand the situation while knowingly engaging in disruptive behavior and simultaneously demanding preferential treatment.

item.title: Philippine DFA warning exposes divisions regarding China policy: experts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 23:30:00
Illustration: Liu Xidan/GT The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) has publicly warned individual officials, agencies or sectors against "pursuing preferred approaches toward China, or any other international partner, without regard for the consequences on the government's overall policy," stressing that all civilian and uniformed officials must follow the president's foreign policy direction. The statement, issued on Sunday, did not name any specific officials, but has drawn attention from Philippine media amid signs of policy discord within the government over how to manage relations with China, with local outlets singling out Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson Jay Tarriela and Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. In its statement, the DFA described as "regrettable" recent public comments by certain government officials that conflated documentary evidence, public rhetoric and official diplomatic messaging. The DFA warned that portraying diplomatic dialogue as inadequate, counterproductive or secondary to public exposure creates a false choice between diplomacy and transparency, which could erode the Philippines' international credibility and weaken its negotiating position. It stressed that transparency should not displace, constrain or collide with diplomacy. Chinese experts observed that the DFA's statement reflects an internal division within the Philippines regarding its China policy. Certain Philippine officials have prioritized self-serving interests above national interests, and their provocative public remarks disrupt official diplomatic arrangements. The DFA's statement represents an effort to reassert control over foreign policy. Experts caution that China-Philippine ties will see no meaningful improvement if Manila fails to deliver tangible actions, and reckless remarks from individual officials will only add obstacles to bilateral relations. Internal divisions exposed The Manila Standard interpreted the DFA's statement as an apparent reaction to a newspaper column published Saturday by Tarriela on the South China Sea issue, titled "Why Beijing wants us to go quiet." In the article, Tarriela claimed that releasing videos, photographs and information about maritime incidents had helped shape international opinion and sustain support for the Philippines. He said ending these disclosures would reduce global attention to the waters and weaken support for Philippine maritime interests. Philippine news outlet Politiko in a Sunday report suggested that the DFA's statement appeared to be directed at Teodoro. Teodoro criticized Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi following his November 3 telephone conversation with Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, according to The Philippine Star. An opinion article on the Manila Times on Monday called Teodoro "a huge liability" for the Philippine government that is already imploding, urging President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to fire him if only to lighten his burden. Dai Fan, director of the Center for Philippine Studies at Jinan University, told the Global Times on Monday that politicians, including Tarriela and Teodoro, have frequently taken a tough stance on China-related issues, including matters beyond their own duties. Their approach reflects personal political ambitions and attempts to expand their influence rather than considerations for national interests. Dai further noted that the DFA statement exposed a lack of coordination within the Philippines on China policy. "It may signal an effort by the DFA to reassert its role in shaping and coordinating foreign policy, following repeated attempts by the defense establishment to securitize and militarize China-related matters, in order to prevent South China Sea disputes from overriding the full spectrum of bilateral ties," the expert said. The DFA stressed that civilian authorities direct the country's foreign relations, while security agencies provide operational assessments. All government officials must follow the president's policy direction, with professional advice handled through appropriate internal channels, the statement said. Actions awaited The DFA statement came shortly after top diplomats of China and the Philippines held a telephone conversation on November 3. According to the Chinese Foreign Ministry, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi noted that China-Philippines relations were facing malicious disruptions and urged the Philippine side to strengthen restraint over relevant individuals and send a rational and unified voice on its policy toward China. The ministry said the two sides reached basic consensus on improving and developing China-Philippines relations, including agreeing to maintain diplomatic dialogue, making efforts to remove all kinds of interference at home and abroad, opposing any acts of malicious provocation and sabotage against the diplomatic efforts of both sides, responsibly managing differences and stabilizing the situation, and seeking to expand shared interests. The DFA reaffirmed its account of the November 3 telephone conversation, describing it as part of efforts to maintain stable and predictable bilateral relations while managing differences responsibly, according to the Manila Standard. Ding Duo, director of the Research Center for International and Regional Issues at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told the Global Times that in the Philippines, diplomatic officials seemingly favored dialogue to prevent maritime tensions from dominating bilateral relations, while some military and coast guard officials advocated for a tougher and more provocative approach toward China. Dai noted it remains to be seen whether the DFA's statement could effectively coordinate internal division and rein in provocative elements. The Marcos administration may be pursuing a two-pronged tactic: letting defense agencies sustain a hardline posture while diplomats seek de-escalation. Such a dual-track strategy, however, would severely damage the government's policy credibility, the expert warned. In its statement, the DFA also said the November 3 exchange was part of efforts to maintain stable bilateral relations and secure a conducive regional environment before, during and beyond the ASEAN and APEC meetings. The Philippine diplomatic establishment hopes to prevent maritime disputes from disrupting high-level exchanges and regional agendas, reflecting its willingness to stabilize bilateral relations. However, whether this will translate into concrete actions remains to be seen, Ding said. Grassroots calls heard Business and civil society voices push for healthy China ties. Against the backdrop of official discord, Philippine business and civil society groups are calling for sustained diplomatic engagement with China. Tourism data cited by BusinessMirror on October 28 showed strong momentum in people-to-people exchanges: 234,953 Filipinos traveled to China in the first nine months of 2026, a 51.04 percent year-on-year jump, far outpacing the 7.16 percent rise in the country's total outbound travel. On November 7, 20 organizations representing labor, business, and civil society expressed support for the DFA's efforts to maintain dialogue and cooperation with China, citing the importance of bilateral relations for trade, exports, tourism and overseas Filipino workers. Their appeal followed an earlier call from Philippine business and sectoral groups that warned against public recriminations and inflammatory rhetoric, and urging both sides to return to established diplomatic channels. Dai said these appeals reflect a growing cohort within Philippine society advocating a more balanced China policy. Allowing security priorities and individual or institutional interests to dominate Manila's China strategy will ultimately hurt the Philippines' national and public interests. A stronger coordinating role for the DFA, paired with greater heed to civil society and business voices, could foster a more rational, balanced approach toward China. Ding cautioned that inconsistent policy messaging from Manila leaves China and regional states guessing about the Philippines' true foreign policy direction. The crux lies in whether Manila can turn its commitments into tangible action: scaling back maritime friction and reining in certain politicians' confrontational rhetoric, and refraining from hyping South China Sea disputes at multilateral regional forums.

item.title: China extends pause on US tariffs, unreliable entity list measures on certain US firms; experts urge Washington to honor commitments
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 23:08:00
File photo: China US China announced on Monday that it would extend the suspension of several trade measures against the US for another two months. This extension covers additional tariffs, special port fees, export controls on 16 American entities, and measures against another 11 companies on its unreliable entity list, as the two countries continue to implement agreements reached through high-level meetings and economic and trade consultations. These moves came as Washington also extended the suspension of certain trade restrictions involving China, including measures targeting its maritime industry and the expansion of export controls to affiliates of listed entities. This followed a high-level China-US economic and trade video call on Friday, during which both sides agreed to strengthen cooperation and properly manage differences. Chinese experts said that the latest policy actions demonstrate China's commitment to implementing the consensus reached by the two leaders and reflect continued efforts by both sides to maintain stability in economic and trade relations. While the extensions could help reassure businesses and create room for further negotiations, they urged Washington to stop using new restrictions as bargaining leverage and to work with China to preserve the progress already made. From consensus to action Under a notice issued by the Customs Tariff Commission of the State Council, China will continue suspending a 24 percent additional tariff on US imports for another two months from 1:01 pm on Tuesday, while retaining a 10 percent additional tariff. This decision was made to implement the consensus reached during the China-US leaders' meeting in Washington, the commission said. In a separate explanation, the commission's office noted repeated US statements about plans to replace tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which it said had been ruled invalid, with tariffs under Section 301 of US trade law. China will closely monitor subsequent US measures and adjust its corresponding tariff countermeasures as appropriate. The office said that the extended suspension would provide a more stable and predictable environment for bilateral business cooperation and help promote the sustained improvement of China-US economic and trade relations. Separately, China's Ministry of Transport announced it would continue to suspend special port fees on US-linked vessels for another two months, until January 10, 2027. The ministry will also continue to suspend the launch of an investigation into the impact on the security and development interests of China's shipping, shipbuilding and related industrial and supply chains. In two further announcements, China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said that it would extend the suspension of export control measures targeting 16 US entities and restrictions on 11 other US entities on its unreliable entity list for another two months, starting Tuesday. Both decisions were made to implement the outcomes of the eighth round of China-US economic and trade consultations, the ministry said. Under the arrangements, exporters seeking to supply dual-use items to the 16 US entities must apply to MOFCOM for licenses, while Chinese companies seeking to trade with the other 11 entities may apply for approval. Applications meeting the relevant requirements will be approved, the ministry said. China's concrete policy actions demonstrate its commitment to honoring the consensus reached by the two countries' leaders and its sincerity in maintaining stable economic and trade relations with the US, while reflecting a constructive approach to managing differences and creating favorable conditions for further bilateral negotiations and cooperation, experts noted. The latest measures build on a joint arrangement reached during China-US trade talks in Kuala Lumpur in October 2025, under which the US agreed to keep its 24 percent additional tariffs on Chinese goods suspended for a year, with China adjusting its countermeasures accordingly. The two sides agreed in September to extend the broader arrangement until January 10, 2027. The US has also taken steps to maintain some existing arrangements. In notices issued on Friday, the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) extended 178 exclusions from Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods until January 10, 2027, and prolonged the suspension of measures targeting China's maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors through 11:59 pm Eastern Time on January 9, 2027. Separately, the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security extended the suspension of its rule expanding export controls to affiliates of certain listed entities through January 10, 2027. The extension took effect on November 9, according to the US Federal Register. The two-month extension could help ease cost pressures and stabilize expectations for fourth-quarter export orders, although it represents a temporary reprieve rather than a broad easing of tariffs, according to market analysts. The International Chamber of Shipping on November 2 welcomed a US proposal to extend the suspension of port fees on China-linked vessels, calling it "a very positive development" for US businesses and consumers that could pave the way for a lasting China-US agreement. The latest measures showed that both countries were translating the consensus reached by their leaders into concrete policies, said Song Guoyou, deputy director of the Center for American Studies at Fudan University. "These steps show that both sides are honoring their previous trade commitments, helping build confidence in implementing existing agreements and laying a positive foundation for the next round of economic and trade talks," Song told the Global Times on Monday. Cheng Dawei, a professor at the School of Economics at Renmin University of China, said that the two-month extension could help ease concerns about major trade frictions in the near term. "Amid growing global uncertainty, these concrete policy actions by both countries provide an anchor of stability for markets," she noted. Uncertainty over the direction of US policy remained particularly pronounced amid political adjustments following the midterm elections. Against this backdrop, maintaining a degree of stability in bilateral trade would give businesses greater predictability in planning trade, investment and supply-chain activities, according to Cheng. Stability under pressure Despite progress in implementing previous China-US trade agreements, Washington has continued to impose or propose restrictions on Chinese businesses in areas including technology, outbound investment and biotechnology, casting uncertainty over the prospects for lasting stability in bilateral trade ties. On Friday evening, Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, China's lead official for economic and trade affairs with the US, held a video call with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The two sides held candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on implementing the consensus reached by their leaders during meetings in Beijing and Washington, as well as the outcomes of previous trade consultations. During the call, China also expressed serious concerns over recent US economic and trade restrictions, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Saturday. On Thursday, the US State Department announced sanctions against two Chinese companies over alleged links to Cuba. MOFCOM strongly opposed the move on Saturday, saying that Washington had intensified sanctions and introduced discriminatory restrictions that seriously harmed Chinese companies' legitimate rights and interests. The ministry urged Washington to correct its actions, reserving the right to take necessary measures to protect China's interests. Song noted that the contrasting developments reflected a dual approach in Washington's China policy: implementing commitments in areas where agreement had been reached while continuing to exert pressure elsewhere in pursuit of additional bargaining leverage. "Such an approach is not conducive to the long-term stability of China-US economic and trade relations," Song said. He urged Washington to change its mind-set, prioritize stability and address differences through sincere and constructive dialogue rather than tactical pressure. Cheng said that Washington's willingness to compromise varied across sectors. There was greater room for negotiation in areas where the US faced less competitive pressure, but reaching agreements remained more challenging in fields involving intense technological and industrial rivalry. She also cautioned that uncertainty surrounding US domestic politics could complicate the outlook. While recent agreements had helped establish a degree of stability, substantive progress would require the two sides to address more difficult issues where differences remained. Attention is also turning to the upcoming APEC meetings in Shenzhen. Chinese and US negotiators had been working toward further trade and investment arrangements ahead of the meetings, although differences remained over parts of the proposed package, the South China Morning Post reported on October 20, citing sources familiar with the discussions. Cheng highlighted the importance of high-level diplomacy in stabilizing bilateral ties and strengthening market confidence. Further high-level engagement, if it takes place, could help advance cooperation and send a positive signal amid global uncertainty, she said. A constructive approach to resolving differences would help build on recent progress and create conditions for more stable China-US economic and trade relations, according to Song.

item.title: New BCI and neuromodulation technologies help military pilots combat mental fatigue, enhance performance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 21:23:00
Photo: Screenshot from CCTV From brain-computer interfaces (BCI) and neuromodulation to advanced flight training technologies, an aerospace medicine summit hosted by the Air Force Medical University over the weekend in Xi’an, Northwest China’s Shaanxi Province, showcased the latest advances in aerospace medicine, flight training, and aeromedical rescue, China Central Television (CCTV) reported on Sunday. More than 1,000 experts and scholars from across China, including the military, gathered to discuss key challenges and cutting-edge developments with the aim of advancing high-quality scientific and technological innovation in aerospace medicine, according to CCTV. At this year's forum, a key topic of discussion was the application of BCI and neuromodulation technologies to strengthen aircrew members' physical and psychological resilience and sustained combat effectiveness under high-intensity missions. Experts discussed ways to protect aircrew from extreme physical and psychological stress, improve personnel selection and training, and leverage digital intelligence to enhance aviation capabilities. Yang Liu of the Air Force Medical University said pilots undergo training using breathing exercises and biofeedback before missions. Between missions or afterward, brief and safe transcranial microcurrent stimulation can be used to modulate brain regions associated with cognitive functions, helping pilots quickly alleviate mental fatigue. In addition, efficient personnel selection and training, as well as the integration of digital intelligence technologies, were among the key topics discussed at the forum. The forum also highlighted advanced flight training technologies, including a spatial disorientation simulator that recreates illusions encountered during night flights and when flying through clouds. The immersive system helps pilots maintain spatial awareness and better control their aircraft, enhancing flight safety. For example, when some pilots conduct training exercises in the deserts of northwest China, both the night sky and the ground can be completely dark due to the absence of artificial lighting. Pilots may experience spatial disorientation, mistaking the ground for the sky and vice versa, posing serious safety risks. Specialized ground-based simulators recreate realistic flying environments to help pilots recognize and respond to such illusions effectively. The forum also featured innovations in cognitive computing and non-invasive BCI aimed at enhancing aircrew operational capabilities, including an attention assessment and training system. The system uses real-time eye-tracking and physiological data to monitor pilots' attention distribution, cognitive workload and stress levels in complex environments. Models based on expert knowledge automatically score performance, helping trainees identify weaknesses and undertake targeted training, driving a shift in cognitive skills training from experience-based instruction to data-driven training supported by digital technologies. In addition, emerging forms of information-driven, intelligent and unmanned warfare are changing combat injury patterns and casualty evacuation conditions, creating new challenges for aeromedical rescue and rapid treatment. Wang Jianqi of the Air Force Medical University said researchers had developed the Chinese military's first casualty-search drone. They had also made advances in using drones to inject emergency medication into injured personnel at distant locations, buying time for treatment. Advances in unmanned technologies are making unmanned equipment an increasingly important part of aeromedical rescue, helping overcome the limitations of traditional rescue operations. Global Times

item.title: DPP slammed for politicizing Sun Yat-sen's commemorations amid fears of failed 'de-Sinicization' agenda: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 21:19:00
The documentary Sun Yat-sen Photo: CCTV News A historical documentary on the forerunner of China's anti-feudalism revolution, Sun Yat-sen, began airing on China Central Television (CCTV) on Sunday, ahead of mainland commemorations marking the 160th anniversary of his birth on Thursday. The release comes amid the Taiwan authorities' move to discourage people on the island from attending commemorative events on the mainland, which a Chinese expert said exposes the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' fear that their "de-Sinicization" agenda could fail, as well as their politicization of shared historical memory. Such efforts would ultimately prove futile in the face of the overwhelming trend toward national reunification, the expert said. The documentary, titled Sun Yat-sen, traces the revolutionary leader's life and career through historical records and archival materials. The documentary explores Sun's patriotism, revolutionary commitment, and vision for national progress, while highlighting the contemporary significance of his ideals in promoting solidarity among Chinese people at home and abroad, advancing peaceful development of cross-Straits relations, and realizing national reunification, according to CCTV News. The Standing Committee of the 14th Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) National Committee previously adopted a decision on holding commemorative events on the occasion of the 160th anniversary of the birth of Chinese revolutionary and statesman Sun Yat-sen. However, Taiwan's so-called "Mainland Affairs Council (MAC)" recently said that applications from people on the island who require official permission to travel to the mainland to attend the events would not be approved. It also urged people from other sectors not to travel to the mainland, Hong Kong, or Macao special administrative regions to participate in or co-organize related activities. The DPP authorities were politicizing shared historical memory and using the pretext of "united front" activities to discourage cross-Straits exchanges, Zhang Wensheng, deputy dean and a professor at the Taiwan Research Institute at Xiamen University, told the Global Times on Monday. Zhang attributed the move to the DPP's pro-independence political mindset, saying it reflected concerns that closer contact with the mainland could strengthen Taiwan residents' sense of shared identity with people across the Straits and their identification with the concept of one China. "Their concern is that Taiwan residents may see for themselves that many of the visions Sun Yat-sen outlined have been realized on the mainland," Zhang said. He added that the DPP authorities feared their "de-Sinicization" agenda could collapse, as it would ultimately prove futile in the face of the overwhelming trend toward national reunification. Sun's legacy of seeking national salvation, promoting democracy, and revitalizing China continues to resonate with people on both sides of the Straits. Sun initiated the 1911 Revolution and advanced the Three Principles of the People, while also promoting cooperation with the Communist Party of China (CPC), the expert noted. Sun remains widely respected on the island of Taiwan, where he is traditionally referred to as the "Father of the Nation," Zhang said. Commemorating Sun today should involve reflecting on his aspirations to save the country, safeguard national unity, and revitalize China. By discouraging participation in the mainland commemorations, the DPP authorities were acting contrary to the spirit of Sun's legacy, the expert said. He added that the MAC's claim that Sun's political ideals differed from those of the Communist Party of China (CPC) was untenable. In response to the MAC's claim, spokesperson Zhu Fenglian of the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office said at a press conference on November 4 that promoting national reunification and national rejuvenation were ideals that Sun had pursued throughout his life. Chinese Communists were the most resolute supporters, most loyal collaborators, and most faithful successors of Sun's revolutionary cause, Zhu said. Under the leadership of the CPC, the Chinese people had made widely recognized achievements over more than a century of struggle, with many of the blueprints envisioned by Sun having become reality, she added. Zhu slammed the DPP authorities for betraying Sun's legacy and disrespecting his character, saying that history could not be betrayed and that national reunification was an inevitable trend.

item.title: Is investigation into Jensen Huang about counter-espionage, or is it a political witch hunt?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 15:50:00
Jensen Huang. Photo: VCG One woman, one affair, and a national security narrative that the American media have spun with more imagination than evidence. That was all it took to thrust one of US' most powerful tech CEOs into the middle of a "spy" controversy. On Sunday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair - but whether this marks the end of the media storm or just the beginning remains to be seen. It started with an accusation from The New York Times. Beginning with its October 29 article and continuing in a series of follow-ups, the newspaper claimed that a woman who had held an executive role at a Singapore-based data center company was suspected of working for China's military and top spy agency. According to the reports, she had developed a "close relationship" with Huang and allegedly helped China obtain advanced AI chips subject to US export controls. Western media quickly jumped on the story. Suddenly, it had all the ingredients of a political spy thriller: Chinese intelligence agencies, cutting-edge AI chips, alleged corporate infiltration, an intimate personal relationship, and the head of one of the US' most vital tech companies. It's quite a story, complete with all the twists and suspense of a Hollywood thriller. But so far, the public has seen no hard evidence to back up the central allegations. The key claims in the media reports rely heavily on anonymous sources and materials that the media could not verify. China's Foreign Ministry rejected the allegations on October 30, calling relevant report unsubstantiated and nothing but smears against China. The ministry reiterated the statement on Monday. The Ministry of Home Affairs of Singapore has also rejected a Wall Street Journal report citing sources who said Singapore officials had concerns about, and had investigated, a businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. It stated that neither the Singapore Government nor its officials said this and there were no such investigations. Meanwhile, the political stakes in Washington keep rising. On Sunday, the NVIDIA Board announced an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. However, it also stressed that the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised. Additionally, three House chairmen want Huang to brief them privately on November 18. Who are these anonymous sources cited by the American media? Where is the hard, independently verifiable evidence? Why are these allegations surfacing now? And perhaps most importantly, who stands to benefit? For now, none of these questions has a clear answer. But one thing is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: Huang is no longer simply weathering a media storm over his private life; he is facing a controversy with unmistakable political overtones. The episode is beginning to follow a familiar pattern of political targeting: US media outlets amplify the claims allegedly supplied by insiders and frame them as a national security threat; politicians pile on; and before any investigation has reached its conclusions, the court of public opinion has already begun passing judgment. One fact should not be overlooked. In an environment where US competition with China is increasingly politicized, Chinese heritage can turn ordinary business ties into objects of political suspicion. Huang is a US citizen. The company he leads is a pillar of the US' AI strength. Yet he has been swept into a media storm over alleged Chinese intelligence activity. This raises a pointed question: when an American entrepreneur's business network intersects with China, is he seen first as an American entrepreneur - or first as an ethnic Chinese person who must face extra scrutiny? There is another backdrop that cannot be ignored: political infighting. Political divisions in the US over AI development are widening. The current administration is pushing hard on AI investment and data-center construction. Some Democrats, however, want to slow that expansion, citing concerns over energy use, environmental impact, and the power of tech giants. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has long pressed Huang to testify on Nvidia's China-related business and its approach to export controls. Those efforts were previously limited by procedural hurdles, including subpoena power. After Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress, would the path to similar investigations and subpoenas become significantly smoother? A country's technological competitiveness ultimately rests on innovation, talent, and confidence in its own institutions. When the heads of the US' leading tech companies must, beyond normal commercial activity, continuously pass political loyalty tests that lack clear standards, it reveals a deeper anxiety in the US about the global AI race. Suspicion alone will not produce the next generation of GPUs. Over-politicizing scrutiny and the habit of framing business ties as security risks will not win the next round of AI competition. The truly strong are busy building what comes next. Only those growing more anxious go looking for enemies nearby.

item.title: Pakistani astronaut's participation in Shenzhou-24 mission to mark first visit by a foreign astronaut to China Space Station: FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 15:50:00
China's Shenzhou-21 and the Tiangong space station in the orbit Photo: IC China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners. Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program. The Pakistani astronaut will be the first foreign astronaut to step into China's space station, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Guo made these remarks in response to a question at Monday's regular press conference about a Pakistani astronaut's planned participation in the Shenzhou-24 crewed mission as a payload specialist. The astronaut is expected to return aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft after completing a short-term stay in orbit. Guo said that exploration of the vast universe and peaceful use of outer space are humanity's shared pursuit and bear on the welfare of all peoples. China advocates the peaceful use of outer space, engages in active international space cooperation, and promotes the building of a community with a shared future in the domain of outer space, he said. This is yet another key outcome of bilateral cooperation as we mark the 75th anniversary of China-Pakistan diplomatic ties, Guo said. China stands ready to work with the Pakistani side to carry forward our traditional friendship, deepen cooperation in space and other fields, and bring bilateral relations to new heights, Guo added. The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) announced the arrangement on Saturday. In February 2025, China and Pakistan signed a cooperation agreement on astronaut selection, training, and participation in Chinese space station flight missions in Islamabad, officially launching astronaut selection from Pakistan, according to the Xinhua News Agency. After a rigorous three-stage selection and assessment process, two Pakistani reserve astronauts were selected. After completing all training and passing the evaluation in China, one will carry out the crewed flight mission, while the other will serve as a backup. According to the Pakistani local media outlet Dawn, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met the two in April and congratulated them on their selection. He said the space mission was a "matter of pride for the entire nation" and further commended their "round-the-clock efforts" in achieving the milestone. Shehbaz hoped that the space mission would "add new dimensions to the brotherly relationship between Pakistan and China." Global Times

item.title: 14 killed, 60 rescued in apartment fire in North China's Shanxi; property management personnel placed under control: local authorities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 11:33:00
Firefighters work to extinguish a blaze at a high-rise building in Yingze district, Taiyuan, North China's Shanxi Province, on November 8, 2026. Firefighting operations were still underway as of 7 pm. Photo: VCG A fire at an apartment building in Taiyuan, North China's Shanxi Province, has killed 14 people, while 60 others were evacuated or rescued, with management personnel of the property owner and personnel in charge of the property management company been placed under control measures, local authorities said at a press briefing on Monday afternoon, Xinhua reported. The briefing, held by the Publicity Department of the Taiyuan Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, provided an update on the fire at Haosheng International Apartment. The fire broke out at an apartment building in Yingze district, Taiyuan, at 4:59 pm on Sunday. The open flames were extinguished by 7 pm, and search and rescue operations concluded at 8:30 pm, CCTV News reported earlier. At around 7:30 pm on Sunday, firefighters were using high-altitude firefighting equipment to spray water on the fire-hit area near the top of the building to prevent the flames from reigniting, while smoke continued to billow from some floors, a reporter from China National Radio (CNR) reported from the scene. Flashlights could be seen moving behind the windows of the burned floors as rescue personnel searched for people inside. Signboards of several training institutions were visible on the building's exterior. Local residents told the reporter that the building housed several training institutions and was adjacent to a hotel. Following the incident, Taiyuan immediately activated its emergency response plan and set up a task force to oversee rescue and response efforts, with dedicated teams for medical treatment, post-accident arrangements, accident investigation and accountability, and overall coordination. The city has mobilized medical resources across the province and municipality to treat the injured, adopting an individual treatment plan and dedicated support team for each patient, according to the briefing. Authorities are also providing assistance to the families of those killed, offering emotional support to the injured and handling compensation matters. Management personnel of the property owner and personnel in charge of the property management company have been placed under control measures, the briefing said. In response to the accident, Taiyuan will conduct a citywide campaign to comprehensively inspect, identify and address workplace safety risks, with a particular focus on fire safety and high-risk industries, in a bid to prevent similar incidents and protect people's lives and property. Global Times
